about: What preachers preach at the Restday service (Docs/Design/42-money-in-circulation.md, Phase 6): a line a minute from the pulpit, heard by everyone in the church. `places`: the communities a sermon belongs to (its own faith's: the Iron Saint in Ser Ferro, the Tide in Ridgemere, the First Oath in Upper Accord); none, any. A preacher doesn't repeat a sermon within four weeks. `{town}` is the town's name.

sermons.title: The Poor Box
lines: Sit, all of you. The benches are hard, and so is the year; we will be brief with one and kind about the other.
There is a box by the door. You know it. Most of you walk past it the way you walk past a beggar: with your eyes on the floor.
I will tell you what goes into that box. Bread, for the wolf who has none. Bandages, for the one who cannot pay a healer.
Not a penny of it sits. The tenth you give at the reckoning does not sleep in the church's chest; it walks out of this door on four feet.
A pack that lets its weakest starve is not a pack. It is a crowd that happens to be going the same way.
You do not give because the church asks. You give because, one winter, it may be your name on the list.
And if it is, come. Nobody here will ask how you came to be hungry. Only whether you have eaten.
Go out into {town} today with your eyes up. Look at the wolf on the steps. Then look at your own paws, and see that they are the same.
Rest well. Eat well. And mind the box on your way out.

sermons.title: Honest Weights
lines: Good morning. I see a great many shopkeepers this morning; I see a great many of you looking at the door already.
Today I speak about scales. Not the fish kind. The kind with two pans and a little brass weight in each.
Every one of you knows how to put a thumb on a scale. The question has never been whether you can.
A short measure of flour cheats the baker's customer once. It cheats the baker every day after, because nobody comes back.
The town runs on trust as a mill runs on water. Muddy it upstream, and everyone downstream drinks it.
When you sell, sell what you say you sell. When you buy, pay what you said you would pay. That is the whole of it.
There is no clever version of this sermon. There is no clever version of honesty.
Tomorrow the shops open and the scales come out. Let them hang level, and let {town} say so of you.
Go in peace, and go with your thumbs to yourselves.

sermons.title: The Shared Hunt
lines: Come in, come in. Close the door; the wind follows you like a debt.
Before there were towns, there was the hunt. Before there was coin, there was meat, and who got it.
No wolf brings down an elk alone. The one at the throat is only there because six others turned it.
And when it fell, the old ones ate. And the pups ate. And the one who went lame in the chase ate, though he caught nothing.
We have walls now, and shops, and ledgers. But the elk is still the elk. Your bread was turned by many paws before it reached yours.
The farmer who grew the wheat. The miller. The baker. The carter who brought the firewood. The guard who kept the road.
When you eat today, eat like a wolf who remembers the hunt: grateful, and leaving something for the one who could not run.
That is all the law there ever was. The rest is only the paperwork.
Rest, now. The hunt begins again at dawn tomorrow.

sermons.title: For Those Who Have Gone
lines: Sit. Today we keep a little quiet for the ones who are not on these benches anymore.
Some of you have an empty place at the table this year. Some of you set it anyway, out of habit, and then have to clear it again.
I will not tell you they are watching. I do not know that. Nobody who tells you so knows it either.
I will tell you what I do know: everything they taught you, they taught you. That does not go into the ground.
The way you hold a tool. The way you greet a stranger. The song you hum without knowing where you learned it.
Grief is only love that has nowhere to go. So give it somewhere. Give it to the living who loved them too.
If you were left an estate, spend some of it kindly. If you were left nothing, you were left them, for a while, and that was much.
Say their names today, out loud, to somebody in {town} who knew them.
Go gently. Rest is not forgetting.

sermons.title: The Road and Its Dangers
lines: Welcome. I see carters' dust on some of you, and I am glad you made it back to sit in it.
The road between towns is long and the woods beside it are not empty. You all know someone who did not come home.
There are those who say: stay inside the walls, then. Grow fat and safe and small.
But the salt comes from the coast and the iron from the hills. A town that will not travel will not eat.
So we send our carters out, and we pray for them, and we pay the escorts, and that is right.
But hear me: if you meet a stranger on the road who is hurt, you are the escort. There is nobody else coming.
And if you meet bandits, give them the purse and keep your throat. No penny in {town} is worth a widow.
Travel well this week, those who must. Come back to these benches. We will keep your seat.
Go in peace, and go armed, and go together.

sermons.title: The Turning Year
lines: Good morning. Look out of the window as you leave today. Something in the light has changed; it always has, by now.
The year turns whether we notice or not. Planting, growing, harvest, and the long cold, and then planting again.
The farmer cannot hurry the wheat. The beekeeper cannot argue with the frost. They wait, and work, and wait.
We are poor at waiting. We want the harvest before the planting. We want the cure before the hurt.
But there is good in the slow things. The cheese ripens in the dark. The wine needs years. Friendships need more.
Put something by this season. A little grain, a little coin, a kindness someone will remember in the winter.
The barns of {town} were full once and will be again. Between the two lies the work.
Rest today. Tomorrow, the year goes on turning, and you with it.
Go well.

sermons.title: The Tenth
lines: Sit down, sit down. Yes, I am going to talk about money. No, the doors are not locked.
A tenth of what you made this month goes to the church. Another tenth to the town. You grumble at both; I would think less of you if you didn't.
But notice: it is a tenth of what you made. Not of what you took in. The month you lost, you paid nothing. Nobody asked you to.
And notice where it goes. The bread on the alms table was bought from your bakers. The candles from your chandler.
The wages of the hands mending the road came from it, and they spent those wages in your shops on Marketday.
Money is like water in a field. Dammed up, it rots. Let it run, and everything green along its ditch grows.
If you ever see this church sitting on a heap of coin, come and tell me. You will be right to.
Until then, give your tenth with a straight back, and watch where it goes. It goes back to {town}.
Go in peace. And yes, you may grumble on the way home.

sermons.title: On Forgiving
lines: Good morning. Some of you are sitting a long way from someone you used to sit beside. I can see it from here.
Somebody wronged you. Perhaps badly. Perhaps it was a broken promise, or a word that should never have been said.
I am not going to tell you it did not matter. It mattered. That is why it still sits in your chest like a stone.
But a stone you carry long enough becomes part of your gait. You start to limp and forget why.
Forgiving is not saying it was fine. It is saying: I will not carry this any further. Here is where I put it down.
You do not have to say it to them. You do not even have to say it today. But you might look across the benches.
{town} is too small for feuds. Sooner or later you will need each other's help, and it is easier with the stone set down.
Rest, and think on it. That is all I ask.
Go in peace, and perhaps not alone.

sermons.title: The Saint at the Forge
lines: Welcome, children of the Saint. Look up at her: iron in her paws, and no crown on her head.
You know the story. When the river rose and the old city drowned, she did not pray. She went to the forge.
She made nails for the new roofs. Hoops for the barrels that floated the grain across. Hinges for the doors of the poor first, and her own last.
That is why we call her the Iron Saint and not the Golden one. Gold sits. Iron works.
So I ask you: what is your iron? What do you make with your paws that others stand on, sleep under, eat from?
The vintner's cask. The brickmaker's tile on the red roofs of Ser Ferro. The farmer's furrow in the gold fields.
None of it is small. A city is only a great many small things that someone bothered to make well.
Go out and make something well this week, in her name.
The Saint's blessing on your work, and on your rest.

sermons.title: What the Tide Takes
lines: Sit, and listen to the rain. It has been listening to us all week.
The tide comes in twice a day, and twice a day it goes out, and it does not care how important you are.
It took the old quay. It took boats, and the wolves in them. And every morning it gives back the fish we live on.
That is the Tide's bargain: everything given is lent. The catch, the coin, the strength in your back. Lent.
The Houses own the land outside the walls, and the ships, and the ironworks. The Tide does not care. It is waiting for them too.
So hold things loosely. Pay your hands fairly. Mend your nets before they need it.
And when the sea gives you a good week, give something back before it asks.
The bell will ring for the boats at dawn. Be on them, or be on the quay to meet them.
Go with the Tide. It is going anyway.

sermons.title: The First Oath
lines: Welcome to the Chapel of the First Oath. Every one of you is sitting under the words, whether you look up at them or not.
Before the Accord there were packs, and between the packs there was blood. Every border was a grave.
And then someone, whose name we have lost, stood between two packs and said: I will keep the peace between you, and ask nothing for it.
That was the First Oath. Not a law. A promise, made by one wolf, to strangers.
The Wardens keep it now with spears. The Concord keeps it with words. But it began with one wolf's word.
So keep yours. To your neighbour, to your trade, to the stranger in the market who trusted your price.
A promise kept is a brick in the wall around this crater. A promise broken is a brick taken out.
Go out into Upper Accord and keep your word this week. That is all the Oath has ever asked.
Peace be kept.
